newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Court asks Manila to justify oil deregulation.
newsitem.headline: Court asks Manila to justify oil deregulation.

text.p: The Philippine Supreme Court on Tuesday ordered the government to explain in 10 days its decision to fully deregulate the oil industry but did not grant a request to temporarily halt the programme.

Court officials said a further hearing would be held when the government replies to a petition by four opposition congressmen and several rights groups that the move is unconstitutional and will hurt consumers.
Left-wing groups staged street protests and public transport drivers went on a one-day a strike in nearby Angeles city on Saturday when the deregulation scheme took full effect.
Under the programme, the country's three oil companies have the right to set their own prices, ending over two decades of state control.
The petition is the latest in a series of legal challenges to President Fidel Ramos's economic reforms programme.

Earlier this month, the Supreme Court declared void a winning bid by a Malaysian company for the historic Manila Hotel and awarded the contract to a Filipino company, saying the 75-year-old building was a national treasure.
In another blow to the government, an appeals court temporarily halted privatisation of the Manila waterworks system after a petition charged that Ramos's powers to bid off the utility had lapsed.

Another opposition congressman, representing tribal groups, is also asking the Supreme Court to strike down a 1995 law allowing foreign firms to own up to 100 percent equity in local mining projects, saying natural resources were the nation's heritage.
Ramos last weekend accused the Supreme Court of jeopardising the country's reforms programme and of intruding onto the executive's turf.

Filipinos felt the early impact of a deregulated oil industry last weekend when oil firms raised the prices of premium gasoline by an average 41.45 centavos per litre to 11.30 pesos ($0.43). Unleaded gasoline prices were raised by an average of 0.66 centavos to 10.8986 pesos per litre, although prices of most other petroleum products were cut.
